honesty: Educational curriculum authored for Savant — not scraped Wikipedia. Each topic teaches with overview, facts, misconceptions, and related learning.

topics.title: Major grape varieties
topics.overview: Vitis vinifera cultivars differ in ripening needs, skin thickness, acidity, and aromatic precursors. Learning a few anchor grapes unlocks most wine lists.
topics.visualAid: Think of grapes as instruments: same vineyard can sound different depending on which cultivar plays the climate.
facts: Cabernet Sauvignon generally needs more heat accumulation than Pinot Noir.
Riesling’s high acid lets it succeed as dry or sweet wine.
Chardonnay’s neutrality makes winemaking choices unusually visible.
misconceptions: A grape name does not guarantee a single taste — climate and cellar choices matter.
Old World vs New World is a teaching shorthand, not a law of flavor.

topics.title: Wine regions
topics.overview: Regions encode climate, tradition, and law. Studying maps teaches why the same grape tastes different across valleys.
topics.visualAid: Start with latitude bands, then zoom into rivers, slopes, and cooling winds.
facts: Maritime climates often moderate heat spikes.
Continental interiors can show larger day–night swings.
AVA and AOC systems are legal geographies — helpful labels, not flavor guarantees.
misconceptions: Famous regions are not automatically better for every grape.
A regional name on a label does not replace vintage and producer context.

topics.title: Climate and terroir
topics.overview: Terroir is the interaction of climate, soil, terrain, and human choices. Savant emphasizes measurable climate and terrain first — with humility about soil myths.
topics.visualAid: Heat accumulation, frost timing, and aspect often explain more beginner mysteries than soil color alone.
facts: Growing degree days summarize heat available for ripening.
Cool nights can preserve acidity even when days are warm.
Slope and aspect change solar exposure and cold-air drainage.
misconceptions: Soil type alone rarely dictates a single flavor note.
Terroir is not a marketing synonym for ‘expensive’.

topics.title: Growing conditions
topics.overview: Vines need a growing season long enough to ripen fruit without excessive disease or freeze damage. Water, wind, and humidity shape both quality and risk.
topics.visualAid: Imagine a balance beam: heat on one side, disease and frost risk on the other.
facts: Spring frost can destroy young shoots.
High humidity raises fungal disease pressure.
Drought stress can concentrate flavors but also reduce yields.
misconceptions: More heat is not always better — some grapes lose freshness.
Irrigation is neither universally good nor bad; context matters.

topics.title: Wine production overview
topics.overview: From harvest to bottle, choices about crush, fermentation vessel, temperature, and aging shape texture and aroma as much as the vineyard.
topics.visualAid: Farm → ferment → élevage → bottle — each stage can amplify or mute site character.
facts: Yeast converts sugar to alcohol and CO₂.
Skin contact builds color and tannin in reds.
Oxygen management influences freshness versus nutty development.
misconceptions: ‘Natural’ is not a regulated synonym for unsupervised.
Oak barrels do not automatically mean better wine.

topics.title: Fermentation
topics.overview: Fermentation temperature, yeast, and vessel change ester profiles and texture. Understanding fermentation demystifies ‘funky’ versus ‘clean’ styles.
topics.visualAid: Cooler ferments often keep delicate aromatics; warmer ferments can deepen color extraction in reds.
facts: Stuck ferments leave residual sugar unexpectedly.
Carbonic maceration favors early-drinking fruitiness (classic Beaujolais lesson).
Lees contact can add texture after primary fermentation.
misconceptions: All fermentation smells are faults — some are stylistic.
Alcohol level alone tells you little about quality.

topics.title: Oak aging
topics.overview: Oak can add vanilla, spice, and texture while allowing controlled oxygen exchange. Toast level and barrel age matter.
topics.visualAid: New oak is a loud instrument; neutral vessels are quieter stages.
facts: French and American oak differ in lactone and toast character.
Larger, older vessels impart less flavor.
Stainless steel preserves primary fruit when oxygen is limited.
misconceptions: More oak is not a quality score.
Unoaked wines are not incomplete — they are a stylistic choice.

topics.title: Malolactic fermentation
topics.overview: Bacteria convert malic acid to softer lactic acid. Common in reds; optional in whites — a key reason some Chardonnays taste creamy.
topics.visualAid: Sharp green-apple acidity can round into yogurt-like softness when MLF completes.
facts: MLF is a bacterial process, not alcoholic fermentation.
Diacetyl can contribute buttery notes.
Blocking MLF keeps wines tenser and fresher.
misconceptions: Butter equals poor wine — it can be intentional.
All white wines undergo MLF.

topics.title: Sparkling production
topics.overview: Bubbles come from trapped CO₂. Traditional method builds complexity via bottle fermentation and lees aging; tank method emphasizes fruit and efficiency.
topics.visualAid: Pressure + time on lees ≈ texture lesson in a glass.
facts: Dosage adjusts final sweetness after disgorgement.
Autolysis contributes brioche notes over time.
Prosecco often uses tank method; Champagne requires traditional method by definition.
misconceptions: All sparkling wine is Champagne.
Sweeter sparkling is always lower quality.

topics.title: Fortified and dessert wines
topics.overview: Fortification adds spirit; dessert styles concentrate sugar through late harvest, botrytis, or freezing. Acidity is the balancer.
topics.visualAid: Sweetness without acid collapses; acid without fruit tires — balance is the lesson.
facts: Port styles differ by oxidative aging path.
Sherry teaches biological versus oxidative aging.
Ice wine requires deep cold at harvest.
misconceptions: Sweet wine is only for beginners.
High alcohol always means dessert wine.

topics.title: Food pairing
topics.overview: Pairing works through weight, acid, salt, fat, spice, and aromatic bridges — not rigid color rules.
topics.visualAid: Match intensity: delicate wine with delicate food; rich with rich — then use acid to cut fat.
facts: High acid wines refresh salty and fried foods.
Tannin loves protein and fat.
Spice heat often prefers off-dry aromatics.
misconceptions: Red meat must pair with red wine always.
There is one correct pairing for each dish.

topics.title: Glassware and serving temperature
topics.overview: Glass shape and temperature change aroma delivery and perceived body. Small adjustments teach more than expensive stemware myths.
topics.visualAid: Too cold mutes aroma; too warm exaggerates alcohol.
facts: Many light reds benefit from a slight chill.
Sparkling stays lively cooler than still whites.
A clean, tulip-shaped glass outperforms novelty shapes for learning.
misconceptions: One universal glass ruins all wine equally — still, consistency helps tasting practice.
Room temperature always means 72°F / 22°C for reds.

topics.title: Storage and aging
topics.overview: Stable cool temperature, darkness, and humidity protect wine. Most wine is meant to be enjoyed young; aging potential is grape-, region-, and vintage-dependent.
topics.visualAid: Think pantry calm, not fridge freeze-thaw cycles.
facts: Heat spikes permanently damage wine faster than mild cool storage.
UV light can create lightstrike faults.
Drink windows are estimates, not clocks.
misconceptions: All wine improves with decades.
A wine fridge is required to enjoy wine at all.

topics.title: Wine faults
topics.overview: Faults are unwanted aromas or textures from spoilage, packaging, or winemaking accidents. Learning faults prevents blaming the grape unfairly.
topics.visualAid: Cork taint (TCA) mutes fruit; volatile acidity smells like vinegar or nail polish in excess.
facts: TCA is often cork-related but not exclusively.
Reduction can smell sulfurous and sometimes blows off with air.
Brettanomyces is stylistic for some, a fault for others — context matters.
misconceptions: Any unfamiliar smell is a fault.
A flawed bottle means the entire vintage is bad.

topics.title: Tasting methodology
topics.overview: See → smell → taste → conclude. Structured tasting builds memory without turning preference into a scoreboard.
topics.visualAid: Write three words you actually perceive before borrowing fancy vocabulary.
facts: Acidity is tasted on the sides of the tongue as mouthwatering freshness.
Tannin dries the gums and cheeks.
Personal preference is valid data — separate it from description.
misconceptions: Experts never disagree.
Points are required to learn.
